content: Materials that are stored, utilized, or transported should be managed effectively to support health emergency and disaster risk management. Existing facilities should undergo safety assessments, and corrective actions should be implemented as needed. All health facilities must be prepared to respond to both internal and external emergencies. Efforts should be made to establish and promote regional, subregional, and interregional collaboration within the World Health Organization (WHO). This includes sharing expertise and experiences to enhance capacity in risk reduction, emergency response, and recovery. The role of the local health workforce in emergency management systems should be strengthened by providing leadership, health services, and access to resources, alongside comprehensive planning and training for healthcare workers. Member States, donors, and development partners are urged to allocate sufficient resources to health emergency and disaster risk management programs. This includes international cooperation, humanitarian appeals, and support for WHO’s role in these efforts. The evidence base for health emergency and disaster risk management should be expanded through operational research and economic assessments. National and subnational risk assessments should be supported to catalyze action and strengthen capacities for disaster risk reduction. Progress on these initiatives should be reported to the World Health Assembly. In emergency situations, the rapid provision of medical supplies, including controlled substances such as narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances, is often hindered by regulatory requirements for import and export. This delay can exacerbate human suffering by depriving individuals of adequate pain relief and sedation. Simplified regulatory procedures are urgently needed to facilitate the timely international transportation of these essential medicines during emergencies. The International Narcotics Control Board (INCB) has recommended that, in emergency situations, control obligations be limited to the authorities of exporting countries. This principle has been endorsed by the United Nations Commission on Narcotic Drugs and the World Health Assembly. WHO has been tasked with preparing model guidelines to assist national authorities in implementing simplified regulatory procedures for the international provision of controlled medicines in emergencies. Suppliers of controlled medicines for humanitarian assistance should meet specific criteria, including experience in providing high-quality emergency medical supplies, adequate stock levels, and knowledge of international drug control conventions. In emergencies, operators requesting controlled substances must provide detailed information about the nature of the emergency, the intended use of the medicines, and the responsible parties for their receipt and distribution. Suppliers must notify the control authorities of the exporting country about each shipment and submit annual reports on emergency deliveries. Control authorities in the receiving country should be informed of the shipments and have the right to refuse their importation if necessary. The integration of palliative care and symptom relief into humanitarian responses is essential. Training programs for responders should cover topics such as pain management, psychological support, and ethical considerations in end-of-life care. These efforts aim to address the disproportionate suffering of vulnerable populations during emergencies and maximize the number of lives saved. In summary, the timely provision of essential medicines, including controlled substances, is critical for effective humanitarian disaster relief. Simplified regulatory procedures, collaboration among stakeholders, and the integration of palliative care into emergency responses are necessary to alleviate human suffering and improve outcomes in crisis situations.
